doc.title: Dick Griffin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 12, 2024

title: Kirk as a force of nature, and what he taught Griffin
summary: Rowe recalls seeing Kirk in Rochester; Griffin recalls Kirk's Christmas gifts and teaching him circular breathing.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: There’s a descriptive phrase that’s sometimes over-used and that is “a force of nature” but I saw Rahsaan in a Rochester club, probably 1970, and that’s how he struck me, as a force of nature — it was just incredible. And I think a lot of people in the audience, after one of his more — I won’t say outlandish — but he was covered with instruments, right, and he’s playing three things at once, and then he finished this song and there was this like small amount of applause. And he took the mic and he goes, “Thanks for that pitter patter.”
We didn’t know what to think, I think people were a bit in shock.

Um hum. He was so smart, I was saying, and he would — if he was alive today I’m sure he would be talking about the politics and all the stuff that’s going on. He would be addressing that and everything. But that’s the smart part about him. He was very well — how can I say — like he would listen. He’d listen to so much and he could read Braille, and he would either read in Braille or listen to classical music. I’d go over to his house and that’s the other side of it — I got a gift — to this day — a Christmas gift. I carry it in my trombone case that he gave me. And he would give gifts and have people over to his house for Christmas and everything. He was very personal and very, very influential and you know you never — those kind of people never really leave you in a sense, because I always — now just to the day somebody taught me on the trombone — I’m able to do it now, you know the circular breathing and stuff like that. And he did it way back in the ‘70s. He took my horn and he just played and played, circular breathing and everything. And he said, “Give it to me,” and he said, “Dick, you can do it.” And at that time I had no clue. I couldn’t — it took me now these forty years to get to what he had taught me.
